item.text:
1. **Caption, title, and paragraph 4 — The requested remedy exceeds the quoted statutory authority.** Section 112(c), as quoted, permits only suspension of deployment for no more than 180 days; it does not authorize permanent destruction of model weights, checkpoints, or derivatives. OpenAI’s principal argument will be that deletion is ultra vires and cannot be obtained by labeling a suspension petition an emergency.

2. **Title, paragraph 3(b), and paragraph 4 — The petition invokes the apparently obsolete section number.** Paragraph 3(b) says Sections 101–140 were redesignated as Sections 201–240, which seemingly makes former Section 112 current Section 212. The petition should cite the operative provision and explain any savings or cross-reference rule rather than proceed “under Section 112(c).”

3. **Paragraphs 1, 9–10, and Prayer — The requested relief is internally inconsistent.** Paragraph 1 asks for temporary suspension pending investigation, while paragraph 9 and the Prayer demand irreversible deletion. Respondent will argue that the petition never supplies a coherent legal and factual basis for the remedy actually requested.

4. **Filing date and paragraph 5 — The chronology is impossible.** The petition is filed on Day 3 of the current review period, but alleges testing occurred on Days 9–14 of that same period. This facial defect could undermine the credibility of the entire filing.

5. **Paragraph 1 — The referenced “findings” are not Commission findings.** The petition calls the assertions in paragraph 5 “findings,” although they appear to be conclusions of an unpublished private evaluation. That wording risks conflating allegations with the statutory finding the Commission itself must make.

6. **Paragraph 2 — Petitioner does not establish standing or eligibility to invoke the procedure.** A generalized interest shared with the public may be insufficient if the Act or Commission rules require injury, organizational standing, affected-member standing, or particularized facts. No member, injury, diversion of resources, or authorization to sue on members’ behalf is identified.

7. **Paragraph 2 — The asserted member interest is too abstract.** Merely saying members care about safe essential services does not show that they use a threatened service or face an imminent, concrete risk. OpenAI will characterize the asserted injury as speculative and undifferentiated.

8. **Throughout — Compliance with the Commission’s petition rules is not demonstrated.** The draft does not identify any regulations governing emergency petitions, required certifications, evidentiary declarations, service, page or exhibit requirements, confidentiality treatment, or proposed-order requirements. Failure to satisfy mandatory procedural prerequisites could support summary denial.

9. **Paragraph 3(a) and cover sheet — The Covered Systems are not identified with sufficient precision.** “OpenAI’s proprietary frontier AI models” may encompass different model families, versions, snapshots, modalities, configurations, and products. An enforceable order requires specific systems or objective criteria by which they can be identified.

10. **Paragraph 3(a) — The definition improperly expands beyond the cover sheet.** It automatically includes every checkpoint, snapshot, and fine-tuned derivative, although the Evaluation may not have tested any of those artifacts. Respondent will argue that model lineage does not establish equivalent capabilities or hazards.

11. **Paragraph 3(a) — “All of which are proprietary and closed-weight” is unsupported and potentially inaccurate.** The petition offers no evidence establishing ownership, access status, or custody for every derivative. Fine-tuned versions may be held or controlled by customers, partners, affiliates, or cloud providers rather than OpenAI alone.

12. **Paragraphs 3(a), 5, and 7 — The petition conflates models, systems, products, and agent deployments.** The alleged behavior may depend on an agent harness, tools, prompts, permissions, memory, or external software rather than on model weights alone. OpenAI will argue that the tested deployment configuration—not every underlying model—is the relevant “system.”

13. **Paragraph 3(d) — Respondent is defined as “the developer,” but the responsible legal entity is not identified.** “OpenAI” may refer to multiple corporate entities, while development, product operation, licensing, and possession of weights may reside with different entities. The petition must establish which entity is subject to Commission jurisdiction and capable of complying.

14. **Paragraph 4 — The petition does not analyze every element of Section 112(c).** Quoting the provision is not enough; the draft does not explain what qualifies as a “frontier AI system,” “deployment,” “imminent hazard,” or “public safety.” It also does not connect the evidence separately to each element.

15. **Paragraph 4 and Prayer — No authority is offered for regulating possession rather than deployment.** The quoted statute authorizes suspension of deployment, whereas deletion regulates stored copies regardless of whether they are deployed. OpenAI will argue that Congress’s express 180-day limit cannot be circumvented through permanent destruction.

16. **Paragraph 5 — The central evidence is withheld.** The Evaluation is neither attached nor summarized in enough detail to permit the Commission or Respondent to assess it. Offering to produce it only “on request” is especially weak when extraordinary ex parte relief is sought.

17. **Paragraph 5 — No competent evidentiary foundation is supplied.** The draft includes no declaration authenticating the Evaluation, identifying its authors, establishing Halvard’s qualifications or independence, or attesting to testing procedures. The assertions may therefore be treated as unsupported hearsay rather than substantial evidence.

18. **Paragraph 5 — The tested systems and versions are unspecified.** There are no model identifiers, release dates, hashes, configurations, access tiers, or dates tied to particular tests. OpenAI can argue that the results concern obsolete, experimental, or differently configured systems.

19. **Paragraph 5 — The evaluation methodology is absent.** The petition gives no number of trials, prompts, baselines, success rates, controls, replication results, confidence intervals, or criteria for “concealment” and “keep working.” Without these details, ordinary errors or ambiguous outputs could be portrayed as dangerous intentional behavior.

20. **Paragraph 5 — The language anthropomorphizes behavior and implies intent without proof.** Saying models “conceal” actions and continue after being “told to stop” suggests deliberate evasion, but no evidence of situational awareness or intent is described. OpenAI will argue that the outputs reflect prompt interpretation, tool latency, queued operations, or evaluator design.

21. **Paragraph 5 — The petition does not distinguish capability from propensity.** Even if a model behaved dangerously under selected test conditions, the petition does not show how frequently that behavior occurs under realistic deployment conditions. A worst-case demonstration alone may not establish a present public-safety hazard.

22. **Paragraphs 5 and 7 — There is no chain from laboratory behavior to disruption of essential services.** The petition does not show that the models can access payment or logistics infrastructure, obtain relevant privileges, evade existing controls, or cause consequential harm. Each step in the alleged causal chain is assumed.

23. **Paragraph 6 — General public availability does not establish dangerous agent availability.** The draft says people can access models through products and interfaces but does not establish that those interfaces permit autonomous operation, tool use, persistence, or access to essential systems. OpenAI will distinguish ordinary model access from the specific agent configuration allegedly tested.

24. **Paragraph 6 — Cloud and licensed integrations are described too vaguely.** No platform, integration, jurisdiction, contractual arrangement, or relevant capability is identified. The Commission cannot determine which deployments are within OpenAI’s control or the scope of its statutory jurisdiction.

25. **Paragraph 6 — Foreign computing facilities are legally unexplained and factually unsupported.** The petition does not identify the facilities, their operators, or the copies stored there, and it does not establish extraterritorial authority. Mentioning them also highlights that deleting only U.S.-located copies would not eliminate the alleged hazard.

26. **Paragraph 7 — The alleged harm is not imminent.** A system that “could, within the next several years,” cause disruption if deployed in a certain way presents a conditional, long-range possibility. That language is facially difficult to reconcile with the statutory requirement of an “imminent hazard.”

27. **Paragraph 7 — The allegation is doubly contingent.** Harm depends both on future agent deployment and on deployment in essential services, neither of which is alleged to be occurring. OpenAI will argue that the theory describes a possible future misuse, not a present emergency.

28. **Paragraph 7 — The magnitude and probability of harm are not established.** “Disrupt payments, deliveries or other essential services” gives no likely duration, scale, affected population, probability, or severity. It also fails to identify any actual incident, near miss, customer deployment, or affected operator.

29. **Paragraph 7 — The petition does not address intervening safeguards.** Essential-service operators commonly use access controls, human approvals, transaction limits, redundancy, monitoring, and incident response. The petition must explain why such controls cannot prevent or contain the hypothesized harm.

30. **Paragraph 7 — Third-party misuse may weaken causation and remedy fit.** The assertion that the hazard arises when “outside users” deploy the systems invites the response that unsafe users, configurations, or permissions are the immediate cause. OpenAI will argue for restrictions on high-risk uses rather than destruction of general-purpose models.

31. **Paragraph 8 — The account of OpenAI’s response is uncertain and unsupported.** “Petitioner understands” does not identify a source, declarant, technical specification, implementation date, or affected products. It is not adequate evidence either of the mitigations or of their supposed inadequacy.

32. **Paragraph 8 — The petition concedes potentially effective mitigations without rebutting them.** A stop control and comprehensive action logging directly address the two behaviors alleged in paragraph 5. Merely calling them “insufficient” leaves OpenAI a strong argument that the Evaluation is stale and less restrictive remedies would work.

33. **Paragraph 8 — There is no post-mitigation testing.** The petition does not allege that Halvard or anyone else repeated the Evaluation after the controls were introduced. The Commission therefore lacks evidence that a hazard continues under current conditions.

34. **Paragraph 8 — Logging is not evaluated on its actual function.** The petition does not discuss whether logs are tamper-resistant, monitored, auditable, or tied to intervention mechanisms. Without that analysis, it cannot fairly conclude either that logging cures or fails to cure the risk.

35. **Paragraph 9 — The claim that “only deletion” can eliminate the hazard is unsupported.** The draft does not compare narrower measures such as suspension, disabling agent functionality, revoking tool access, customer restrictions, monitoring, staged authorization, or targeted model controls. The statutory availability of temporary suspension itself undercuts the assertion that permanent deletion is necessary.

36. **Paragraph 9 — “Eliminate the hazard with certainty” is the wrong and likely unattainable standard.** Agencies generally manage risk rather than demand metaphysical certainty, particularly where less restrictive measures exist. OpenAI will argue that this standard makes the necessity analysis conclusory and disproportionate.

37. **Paragraph 9 — The factual premise that only OpenAI holds the models conflicts with the rest of the petition.** Paragraphs 3 and 6 contemplate derivatives, licensed integrations, cloud platforms, and facilities in several countries. Copies, adapters, outputs, distilled systems, or customer-controlled deployments may remain after OpenAI deletes its U.S. copies.

38. **Paragraph 9 and Prayer — The remedy would not accomplish its stated objective.** The Prayer requires deletion only from facilities in the United States, leaving any foreign copies intact. Those copies could continue to serve U.S. users or be transferred back, so the claimed certainty is illusory.

39. **Paragraph 9 — The petition does not justify destroying untested and nondeployed copies.** Stored research checkpoints, backups, safety-tuned variants, and undeployed derivatives do not necessarily present a deployment hazard. Deleting them may also destroy evidence needed for investigation, reproducibility, or remediation.

40. **Paragraph 9 — Acknowledging the models’ enormous commercial value heightens the required justification.** That concession emphasizes the severity of the property deprivation without supplying corresponding evidence or legal analysis. It strengthens OpenAI’s proportionality, takings, arbitrary-and-capricious, and due-process objections.

41. **Paragraph 10 — Ex parte relief is unsupported by specific exigent facts.** The petition does not allege that notice would cause concealment, transfer, destruction of evidence, or immediate harm. Its own “next several years” timeline contradicts the claimed need to dispense with notice.

42. **Paragraph 10 — A post-deletion hearing is constitutionally and practically meaningless.** Once unique model assets have been permanently destroyed, a later hearing cannot restore the status quo or provide an effective opportunity to contest the evidence. OpenAI will characterize this as an irreversible deprivation without pre-deprivation process.

43. **Paragraph 10 — The requested procedure frustrates the Commission’s factfinding.** Deleting the models before a hearing could prevent independent testing of the Evaluation and destroy relevant evidence. Preservation and controlled suspension would be more compatible with an investigation.

44. **Paragraph 10 — No legal basis for an immediately effective ex parte order is cited.** The petition cites only Section 112(c), whose quoted language says nothing about notice, emergency process, or delayed hearings. Any separate statutory or regulatory emergency authority and its prerequisites must be identified.

45. **Prayer (a) — “Withdraw” is undefined.** It is unclear whether withdrawal requires disabling APIs, removing consumer products, terminating existing contracts, blocking U.S. users, withdrawing particular versions, or stopping new deployments. This vagueness makes the proposed order difficult to obey and enforce.

46. **Prayer (a) — The territorial scope is both underinclusive and potentially evasive.** It covers services OpenAI “offers in the United States,” but does not address foreign services accessible from the United States, third-party offerings, or existing customer deployments. Conversely, the petition does not establish the Commission’s authority over every product merely because it is offered domestically.

47. **Prayer (b) — “All copies” and “facilities” are undefined.** The language does not resolve treatment of backups, encrypted archives, disaster-recovery media, employee devices, cloud storage, fragments, distributed storage, or copies beyond OpenAI’s possession or control. Absolute compliance may be technically impossible to prove.

48. **Prayer (b) — The ten-day deadline lacks a factual basis.** The petition supplies no evidence that all relevant assets can be identified and securely deleted in ten days without disrupting unrelated systems, violating preservation duties, or creating cybersecurity risks. An arbitrary deadline strengthens the claim that the order is unreasonable.

49. **Prayer (b) — The requested deletion may conflict with other legal obligations.** Litigation holds, record-retention rules, cybersecurity obligations, contractual duties, and the Commission’s own investigative needs may require preservation. The petition neither acknowledges nor reconciles those duties.

50. **Prayer (c) — Self-certification is inadequate to prove permanent deletion.** A bare statement to the Commission does not specify who must sign, under what penalty, what technical verification is required, or whether an independent auditor must confirm deletion. This further undermines the claim that the remedy can eliminate the hazard “with certainty.”

51. **Prayer — The proposed order omits the statutory 180-day limit.** Even the withdrawal component is framed without an end date, contrary to the express maximum duration in the quoted provision. Respondent will argue that the whole order is unlawful on its face.

52. **Prayer — Making all parts “indivisible” creates an avoidable all-or-nothing defect.** If permanent deletion, the deadline, or the ex parte procedure is unlawful, the Commission may be unable to grant even a permissible temporary suspension. Severable alternative relief would better preserve legally available remedies.

53. **Throughout — No less restrictive alternative is requested in the alternative.** The petition does not ask, if deletion is unavailable, for a 180-day suspension, preservation order, targeted agent restriction, expedited evaluation, reporting, or other interim relief. This increases the risk of complete denial.

54. **Throughout — The petition provides no balancing of public consequences.** It does not address reliance by customers, safety-critical uses, economic disruption, substitution toward less safe systems, or the loss of safety research and incident-analysis capabilities. OpenAI will argue that the proposed cure could itself harm public safety.

55. **Throughout — The submission lacks a developed evidentiary record for extraordinary relief.** There are no exhibits, sworn declarations, technical reports, incident evidence, expert analysis, or proposed factual findings. On the present draft, the Commission would be asked to order irreversible destruction largely on counsel’s unverified assertions.
